questions.stem: A teacher draws a Production Possibility Curve on the board and asks the class what every point on it stands for. In about 45 words, explain what each point shows and how this helps enterprises and governments.

markingPoints.description: Every point shows the maximum output that can be produced (1)
That output must come through efficient use of resources by avoiding wastage (1)
This helps in better planning and decision-making by enterprises and the governments (1)

answerScheme.modelAnswer: Every point on a Production Possibility Curve shows the maximum output that can be produced through efficient use of resources by avoiding wastage. Because nothing is wasted, working along the curve helps in better planning and decision-making by enterprises and the governments.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.stem: A town council has one stretch of land that residents want for a park, a school and a market. In about 45 words, explain why the council must decide how to allocate the land, and what its decisions affect.

markingPoints.description: Resources have competing uses (1)
Individuals, enterprises and governments must decide how to best allocate them (1)
These decisions affect the well-being of people and society as a whole (1)

answerScheme.modelAnswer: Resources have competing uses, so individuals, enterprises and governments must decide how to best allocate them. Since resources are limited while wants are unlimited, even nations must plan how to use their resources efficiently. These allocation decisions affect the well-being of people and society as a whole.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.stem: A Class 9 student wants to know why the subject is called Economics at all. Using the Greek roots of the word, show in steps where the name comes from and what it turns out to mean.

markingPoints.description: Economics traced to the Greek word oikonomia (1)
oikonomia stated to be composed of two words (1)
oikos named and translated as 'household' (1)
nemein named and best translated as 'management' (1)
Economics stated to refer to household management (1)

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
Step 1 - The word Economics comes from the Greek word oikonomia.
Step 2 - oikonomia is in turn composed of two words.
Step 3 - The first is oikos, which is usually translated as 'household'.
Step 4 - The second is nemein, which is best translated as 'management'.
Step 5 - So economics refers to household management.

evidence: The word Economics comes from the Greek word oikonomia, which
in turn is composed of two words: oikos, which is usually translated
as ‘household’; and nemein, which is best translated as ‘management’.

Step 3 - Producing millets and pulses saves water, improves soil health and promotes sustainable agriculture.
Step 4 - The opportunity cost of producing sugarcane is the forgone gains from saved water and improved soil health.
Step 5 - The choice is therefore a trade-off between short-term economic gains and long-term sustainability.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.stem:
Priya's family receives a fixed amount of money every month, and Priya has been asked to help split it. Her mother points out that the family's needs never end: food, medicines and school supplies are essential, but there are also wants such as jewellery, entertainment and restaurant meals, and some money must be set aside as savings. Priya notices that her uncle simply picks things on instinct in the shop. Her father tells her that this is not the best way, and that a household which wants its limited resources to last should decide using facts and figures rather than guesswork. Priya decides to work out a plan before the next month begins.

(a) Name the three ways in which Priya's family splits the money it has. (b) What should good decisions rely on instead of guesswork? (c) Priya's uncle picks goods on instinct and still runs short by month end. Using the three ways of splitting the money and what good decisions rely on, explain how Priya's plan can help the family avoid that.

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
(a) Essential items, non-essential items and savings. (1)
(b) Data and analysis, not guesswork. (1)
(c) By fixing an amount for essentials, an amount for non-essentials and a sum for savings, and by checking the facts before spending, the family keeps part of its limited money instead of letting wants use it all. (2)

evidence: For example, families allocate their money for essential items (such
as jewellery, entertainment, and restaurant meals) and savings.
However, good decisions rely on data and analysis, not guesswork.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.stem:
In a town where water is scarce, four people argue about how it should be used: a farmer who wants to irrigate a bigger area, a family that wants more drinking water, a factory owner who wants to expand, and the government, which must plan its expenditure. A student listening to them observes that the water cannot serve every purpose at once. She notices too that the people who must choose are not only the ones who use the water themselves, and that whatever is decided changes the well-being of the whole town. She asks her teacher whether there is a subject that takes decisions like these seriously, and what it calls this situation.

(a) Name the subject the teacher describes. (b) Why must individuals, enterprises and governments decide how to best allocate resources? (c) Two of the four people argue that their own need should come first. Explain why the subject says an allocation decision must be taken with the well-being of people and society as a whole in mind, and not one group's interest alone.

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
(a) Economics. (1)
(b) Because resources have competing uses, so individuals, enterprises and governments must decide how to best allocate them. (1)
(c) Because such decisions affect the well-being of people and society as a whole, the chooser cannot serve one group's interest alone; the effect reaches everyone. (2)

questions.stem:
A district has one stretch of canal water and a fixed area of land, and a planner draws a Production Possibility Curve to show the farmer what is possible. She tells him that every point on the curve stands for the most that can be produced, with nothing wasted, and that the curve lists the different combinations of goods that can be made with the resources already available. She adds that this helps enterprises and the government decide better. The farmer objects that the curve leaves out what he wants to grow. The planner explains that it does not choose for him, but it shows the choice he faces.

(a) What does every point on the Production Possibility Curve show? (b) Name the two kinds of body for which the curve helps better planning and decision-making. (c) The farmer objects that the curve leaves out what he actually wants to grow. Explain why the planner is right that the curve does not settle his choice, and what it does settle for him.

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
(a) The maximum output that can be produced through efficient use of resources without wastage. (1)
(b) Enterprises and the governments. (1)
(c) It does not choose for him, because resources have competing uses that must be allocated. It does settle that every combination on it is attainable at the maximum output. (2)
